goals.goal: rust rustc error[E0502]: cannot borrow `*a` as mutable because `a` is also borrowed as immutable - what does it mean and how do I fix it?

nuggets.text: E0502 occurs when a variable already borrowed with one mutability (mutable or immutable) is borrowed again with a different mutability.
The fix is to ensure there are no other live references to the variable before accessing it with a different mutability.
Moving the mutable use before the immutable borrow is created makes the borrows not overlap and fixes the error.

goals.goal: rustc error[E0382]: borrow of moved value / use of moved value - what causes it and what are the ways to fix it?

nuggets.text: E0382 means a variable was used after its contents have been moved elsewhere.
Assigning a value of a type not marked `Copy` moves it and leaves the original variable unusable.
One fix is to pass a reference (`&`) instead of moving the value.
A mutable reference can be created with `&mut`.
Another fix is to duplicate the value by calling `.clone()` on a type that implements `Clone`.
For your own type, `Clone` can be implemented with `#[derive(Clone)]`.
A type whose members are all `Copy` can be marked `Copy` with `#[derive(Copy, Clone)]`.
If mutable shared ownership is truly required, `Rc` together with `RefCell` can be used.
`RefCell` performs runtime borrow checking.

goals.goal: git says 'fatal: refusing to merge unrelated histories' when I run git pull or git merge. What does it mean and how do I get past it?

nuggets.text: By default, `git merge` refuses to merge histories that do not share a common ancestor.
The override is the `--allow-unrelated-histories` option of `git merge`.
`git pull` also accepts the `--allow-unrelated-histories` option.
The `--allow-unrelated-histories` option is meant for merging the histories of two projects that started their lives independently.
No configuration variable to enable `--allow-unrelated-histories` by default exists or will be added, because this is a very rare occasion.

goals.goal: Node.js Error [ERR_REQUIRE_ESM]: require() of ES Module not supported - what does this error mean and does it still happen on current Node versions?

nuggets.text: `ERR_REQUIRE_ESM` means an attempt was made to `require()` an ES Module.
`ERR_REQUIRE_ESM` is deprecated because `require()` now supports loading synchronous ES modules.
`require(esm)` is no longer behind the `--experimental-require-module` flag as of v23.0.0, v22.12.0 and v20.19.0.
`require()` can only load an ES module that is fully synchronous, i.e. contains no top-level `await`.
If the required ES module contains top-level `await`, `require()` throws `ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE` instead.
A file with a `.mjs` extension can be loaded by `require()` as an ES module.
A `.js` file whose closest `package.json` contains `"type": "module"` can be loaded by `require()` as an ES module.

goals.goal: PostgreSQL ERROR: duplicate key value violates unique constraint, SQLSTATE 23505 - what does this code mean and how can I avoid the error on insert?

nuggets.text: SQLSTATE 23505 has the condition name `unique_violation`.
`INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` simply skips inserting a row that conflicts.
`ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` updates the existing row that conflicts with the row proposed for insertion.
23505 belongs to SQLSTATE Class 23, Integrity Constraint Violation.
Applications should usually test the SQLSTATE error code rather than the textual error message.
For a `unique_violation` the server reports the name of the unique constraint in a separate error field.

goals.goal: I'm getting HTTP 429 Too Many Requests from an API. What does 429 mean and how should my client respond?

nuggets.text: HTTP `429 Too Many Requests` indicates the client has sent too many requests in a given amount of time.
A 429 response may include a `Retry-After` header indicating how long the client should wait before making the request again.
Asking the client to slow down the rate of requests is commonly called "rate limiting".
Rate-limiting restrictions are typically based on the client's IP.
Rate-limiting restrictions can be specific to users or authorized applications.
The 429 status code is defined in RFC 6585, section 4.

goals.goal: Python RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded - what triggers it and can I raise the limit?

nuggets.text: `RecursionError` is raised when the interpreter detects that the maximum recursion depth is exceeded.
`sys.setrecursionlimit(limit)` sets the maximum depth of the Python interpreter stack.
Setting the recursion limit too high can lead to a crash.
The highest possible recursion limit is platform-dependent.
`sys.getrecursionlimit()` returns the current value of the recursion limit.
The recursion limit exists to prevent infinite recursion from overflowing the C stack and crashing Python.
`sys.setrecursionlimit` raises `RecursionError` if the new limit is too low at the current recursion depth.
`RecursionError` derives from `RuntimeError`.

goals.goal: Docker prints 'WARNING: Error loading config file: /home/user/.docker/config.json - stat /home/user/.docker/config.json: permission denied'. What causes this and how do I fix it?

nuggets.text: The error indicates the permission settings for the `~/.docker/` directory are incorrect.
The incorrect permissions on `~/.docker/` come from having used the `sudo` command earlier.
One fix is to remove the `~/.docker/` directory.
The `~/.docker/` directory is recreated automatically after it is removed.
Removing the `~/.docker/` directory loses any custom settings.
Another fix is to change ownership with `sudo chown "$USER":"$USER" /home/"$USER"/.docker -R`.
Permissions can then be set with `sudo chmod g+rwx "$HOME/.docker" -R`.
